title: The Temple's Fall and the Coming of the Son of Man
summary: As Jesus leaves the temple, a disciple admires its great stones, and Jesus predicts that not one will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives he tells four disciples what to expect: deceivers, wars, persecution, the abomination of desolation, a time of great distress, and the coming of the Son of Man in the clouds to gather his elect. He ends by warning that no one knows the day or hour and commanding all his followers to keep watch.
story:
Jesus has spent chapters 11 and 12 in the temple, judging it by an acted sign and by parables and silencing its leaders in debate. Chapter 12 closed with a poor widow putting her last two coins into the temple treasury. Now he leaves the building for the last time in Mark and announces its destruction. The speech that follows, often called the Olivet discourse because it is given on the Mount of Olives, is the longest continuous speech of Jesus in Mark and the last teaching he gives before the passion begins in chapter 14.

The chapter looks past the cross to the life of the church: deception, war, persecution before councils and kings, the preaching of the gospel to the nations, a catastrophe in Judea centered on the temple, and finally the coming of the Son of Man. Mark places it here for two reasons. It lets readers who were living through persecution and the upheavals of the Jewish war (AD 66 to 70) see their own time in the light of Jesus' words. And it prepares the passion. In the next two chapters Jesus himself is handed over, stands before a council and a governor, is beaten, and is abandoned by his friends, while the disciples he told to keep watch fall asleep. The road he describes for his followers is the one he walks first.
historical:
The temple Jesus' disciple admired was the work of Herod the Great, who began rebuilding it around 20 or 19 BC; work on the surrounding complex went on until the early 60s AD. Josephus describes its gleaming white stone and gilded facade (Jewish War 5.184-227; Antiquities 15.380-425), and some Herodian blocks still visible in the retaining walls of the Temple Mount are among the largest building stones of the ancient world. The Babylonian Talmud preserves the saying that whoever has not seen Herod's building has never seen a beautiful building (b. Bava Batra 4a).

The generation after Jesus lived through the events his words describe. Josephus records a series of popular prophets who promised signs of deliverance: Theudas, who around AD 45 promised to part the Jordan (Antiquities 20.97-98); an Egyptian prophet who led a crowd to the Mount of Olives in the 50s, promising that Jerusalem's walls would fall at his command (Antiquities 20.169-172; compare Acts 21:38); and others who led people into the wilderness to see signs (Jewish War 2.259-263). In AD 40 the emperor Gaius (Caligula) ordered his statue set up in the temple. The Syrian legate Petronius delayed, faced with crowds of Jews who said they would die rather than allow it, and Herod Agrippa I persuaded Gaius to withdraw the order before the emperor was murdered in January 41 (Josephus, Antiquities 18.261-309; Philo, Embassy to Gaius). The crisis showed how near the desecration Daniel had described could come again.

The revolt against Rome broke out in AD 66. The Syrian legate Cestius Gallus marched on Jerusalem that autumn and withdrew with heavy losses; Vespasian then subdued Galilee and much of Judea in 67 and 68; Nero's death in June 68 threw Rome into civil war, the year of the four emperors (69), which ended with Vespasian on the throne. His son Titus laid siege to Jerusalem in the spring of 70. Josephus, who watched from the Roman side, describes famine, factional slaughter inside the walls, and the crucifixion of captured refugees before the walls. The temple burned in the late summer of 70; Josephus dates it to the tenth of the month Lous (Av), the same day on which he says Babylon had burned the first temple (Jewish War 6.250), while Jewish tradition remembers both destructions on the ninth of Av (m. Taanit 4:6). Titus then ordered the city and temple razed, leaving only a few towers and part of the wall (Jewish War 7.1-3). Excavations since 1968 along the southern and western walls have uncovered Herodian stones thrown down onto the first-century street below. The Arch of Titus in Rome, built after his death in 81, still shows the temple's lampstand carried in his triumph.

Two more details belong here. Josephus reports that a peasant named Jesus son of Ananias cried woes against the city and the sanctuary from about AD 62 until the siege, was beaten by the Jewish leaders and flogged by the Roman governor, and was killed by a stone from a Roman catapult (Jewish War 6.300-309); Josephus and Tacitus both list portents said to have preceded the fall (Jewish War 6.288-315; Tacitus, Histories 5.13). And the church historian Eusebius records that the Christians of Jerusalem, warned by an oracle, left the city before the war and settled at Pella, east of the Jordan (Ecclesiastical History 3.5.3); Epiphanius repeats the tradition in the late fourth century (Panarion 29.7; On Weights and Measures 15). Historians debate how much of the Pella story is history, but it shows that the early church read verse 14 as a warning that had been heeded.
cultural:
The chapter is written in the idiom of Jewish apocalyptic, a kind of writing found in Daniel and in many Jewish works of the period, such as 1 Enoch and, after the temple's fall, 4 Ezra and 2 Baruch, which were written in response to it. Apocalyptic writing speaks of God's decisive acts in history in cosmic language: the sun darkened, stars falling, heavens shaken. The prophets had used the same language for the fall of empires within history. Isaiah 13:10 applies it to Babylon, Isaiah 34:4 to Edom, Ezekiel 32:7-8 to Egypt, and Joel 2:10 and 2:31 to the day of the LORD. A first reader would neither take such language as a weather report nor dismiss it as mere decoration. It announced that God was acting in a way that shook the world.

The discourse also belongs to the ancient farewell speech, in which a leader facing death gathers his followers, warns them of trials to come, and charges them to be faithful: Jacob in Genesis 49, Moses in Deuteronomy 31 to 33, David in 1 Kings 2, and the Jewish Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs. Jesus speaks two days before Passover (14:1), and the discourse is his testament to the church.

Several images drew on shared Jewish expectation. Birth pains were a prophetic picture for the suffering that comes before God's new age (Isaiah 26:17-18, 66:7-9), and later rabbinic tradition spoke of the birth pangs of the Messiah (b. Sanhedrin 98b). False prophets who give signs and wonders had been named in the law (Deuteronomy 13:1-3). Fleeing to the mountains recalled the Maccabees, who fled to the hills when Antiochus IV desecrated the temple (1 Maccabees 2:28), and the caves and ravines of the Judean wilderness had long been a refuge.

The practical details fit Judea. Houses had flat roofs reached by an outside stair, used for work, sleep, and prayer (Acts 10:9), so a man on the roof could escape without entering the house. A field worker laid his outer cloak aside at the edge of the field, and that cloak was his blanket at night (Exodus 22:26-27). Winter was the season of cold rain, when the wadis flooded and travel on foot was hard. The fig tree, unlike most trees in the land, loses its leaves in winter, and its new leaves appear late, so that tender branches meant summer was close. Jewish reckoning divided the night into three watches (Judges 7:19), Roman reckoning into four, and Mark uses the four popular names: evening, midnight, cockcrow, and early morning. A large household had a doorkeeper whose one task was to stay awake for his master. Finally, the aside in verse 14, “let the reader understand,” reminds us that most early Christians heard the Gospels read aloud in their assemblies (Justin Martyr, First Apology 67), so the reader addressed may be the one reading to the congregation.
literary:
The discourse answers the disciples' two questions in verse 4: when will these things happen, and what will be the sign that they are about to be fulfilled. The answer is shaped by repeated commands. The verb blepete, ‘see to it’ or ‘watch out’, occurs at verses 5, 9, 23, and 33, and grēgoreite, ‘keep watch’, at verses 34, 35, and 37. Almost every paragraph ends in a warning rather than a timetable, and the first word of Jesus' answer is not a sign but a caution against being deceived.

The chapter moves in five parts. Verses 1 to 4 set the scene and pose the question. Verses 5 to 13 describe the ordinary conditions of the time before the end: deceivers, wars, earthquakes, famines, and persecution, which are ‘the beginning of birth pains’ and not yet the end. Verses 14 to 23 describe a specific crisis in Judea, introduced by the abomination of desolation, with urgent instructions to flee. Verses 24 to 27 move into the language of the prophets for the coming of the Son of Man, drawn from Daniel 7:13. Verses 28 to 37 give two short parables, the fig tree and the doorkeeper, and set two sayings side by side: these things will happen within this generation (verse 30), and no one knows that day or hour (verse 32). How those two sayings relate is the chapter's great interpretive question, and the shift from the plural ‘those days’ (verses 17, 19, 24) to the singular ‘that day’ (verse 32) is part of the evidence.

The discourse also frames and foreshadows. It stands between two women: the widow who gives her whole living to a temple about to fall (12:41-44) and the woman who anoints Jesus for burial (14:3-9). Its vocabulary returns in the passion: disciples handed over (verse 9) and Jesus handed over (14:10, 15:1); councils and governors (14:55, 15:1); the hour (verse 32, 14:35, 14:41); the command to watch and the disciples found sleeping (verse 36, 14:37-40); the four watches of the night, which match the Last Supper in the evening, Gethsemane in the night, Peter's denial at cockcrow, and the handing over to Pilate in the morning, as R. H. Lightfoot noted (The Gospel Message of St. Mark, 1950); and the Son of Man coming with the clouds, which Jesus repeats to the high priest (14:62). The darkness of verse 24 returns at noon on Good Friday (15:33).

outline.t: The beginning of birth pains: deception, war, and persecution
The abomination of desolation and the great distress
The coming of the Son of Man
The lesson of the fig tree
No one knows the day or hour: keep watch

doctrines.note: The Son of Man will come “in the clouds with great power and glory” and send out the angels to gather his elect (verses 26 and 27). Christians differ on how much of verses 24 to 27 refers to the events of AD 70, but the church's creeds confess from this and related texts that Christ will come again in glory, and verse 32 guards that confession from every attempt to date it.

Jesus announces that Herod's temple, the appointed place of Israel's worship, will be torn down stone by stone (verse 2). In Mark this completes his judgment on the temple in chapter 11 and prepares the claim, made in mockery at his trial, that he would build another not made with hands (14:58). The center of God's presence is moving to Jesus himself.

Jesus reads Daniel as still speaking (verses 14, 19, 26) and gives predictions that shaped the church's life. The chapter treats prophecy as preparation for faithful living, not as a code for calculating dates: nearly every prediction ends in a command to watch, endure, or refuse deception.

“The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (verse 13). The promise is given to disciples who will be hated, betrayed by family, and dragged before courts. Traditions differ on how endurance relates to God's keeping of the elect (verses 20 and 22), but all agree the verse is both a command and a comfort.

“And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all the nations” (verse 10). In the middle of warnings about war and persecution stands a divine necessity: before the end, the good news goes to the Gentiles, and trials before governors and kings become occasions of witness.

words.note: Grēgoreō, to stay awake, keep watch. It occurs about twenty-two times in the New Testament, six in Mark, all of them in the closing verses of this chapter (34, 35, 37) and in Gethsemane (14:34, 37, 38), where the disciples fail to do it. The standard lexicons give both the literal sense, to be awake, and the figurative sense of being alert and vigilant. In Mark the two senses meet: the parable of the doorkeeper becomes, within hours, the disciples' literal sleep. Watching in Mark is not scanning the news for signs but faithfulness at an assigned post while the master is away.

Blepō, to see, and in the imperative to watch out or beware. It is one of the commonest verbs of sight in the New Testament (about 130 times) and occurs fifteen times in Mark. In this chapter it moves from admiration to warning: ‘Do you see all these great buildings?’ (verse 2), then four times as the command ‘see to it’ or ‘be on your guard’ (verses 5, 9, 23, 33), which marks off the sections of the discourse. The disciple who looked at stones is taught to look at himself.

Ōdin, birth pain, labor. It occurs only four times in the New Testament: here and in Matthew 24:8, of the troubles before the end; in Acts 2:24, where God loosed ‘the pains of death’ in raising Jesus; and in 1 Thessalonians 5:3, of sudden destruction coming like labor on a pregnant woman. The image holds two truths together: the pain is real and cannot be stopped once it starts, and it is the pain of something being born. The prophets used it for Israel's anguish before deliverance (Isaiah 26:17-18, 66:7-9).

Bdelugma, something detestable, an abomination. It occurs six times in the New Testament (Matthew 24:15, Mark 13:14, Luke 16:15, and three times in Revelation). In the Greek Old Testament it often translates the Hebrew shiqquts or toevah, words for idols and idolatrous practices that defile what is holy. The phrase bdelugma tēs erēmōseōs, the abomination that makes desolate, comes from Daniel 12:11 in the Greek and from 1 Maccabees 1:54, where it names the pagan altar Antiochus IV set up in the temple in December 167 BC.

Thlipsis, pressure, affliction, distress. It occurs about forty-five times in the New Testament, most often in Paul, and three times in Mark (4:17, 13:19, 13:24). Its root image is being crushed or squeezed. The New Testament uses it both for the ordinary sufferings of believers, through which they enter the kingdom (Acts 14:22), and, as here, for a distress unmatched since creation, language taken from Daniel 12:1. The same word covers the everyday and the extreme, which keeps the chapter from being only about someone else's future.

Eklektos, chosen, elect. It occurs about twenty-two times in the New Testament, and Mark's three uses all fall in this chapter (verses 20, 22, 27). In the Old Testament Israel is God's chosen people (Isaiah 45:4, Psalm 105:6); here the title belongs to Jesus' followers, and the Son of Man calls them ‘His elect’ (verse 27). God shortens the days for their sake, guards them from final deception, and gathers them at the end. In this chapter election is a word of comfort for the persecuted, not a puzzle for the curious.

Genea, generation, the people living at one time, and more broadly a family, race, or kind of people. It occurs about forty-three times in the New Testament and five times in Mark, and every other time Mark uses it (8:12 twice, 8:38, 9:19) it means Jesus' contemporaries, usually with a note of rebuke. BDAG distinguishes those descended from a common ancestor, a group sharing common characteristics, those living at the same time, and an age or period. Everything in verse 30 depends on this word and on the phrase all these things, which is why interpreters argue about both.

Euangelion, good news, gospel. It occurs about seventy-six times in the New Testament and eight times in Mark (1:1, 1:14, 1:15, 8:35, 10:29, 13:10, 14:9, and 16:15 in the longer ending). In verse 10 it is the one piece of good news in a chapter of warnings, and it is joined to dei, it must: the preaching of the gospel to all the nations is as much a part of God's plan as the troubles. Mark's readers, many of them Gentiles, were themselves the evidence that it was happening.

christ:
In this chapter Jesus speaks as a prophet in the line of Jeremiah and Micah, who foretold the destruction of the first temple (Jeremiah 7:12-14, 26:18; Micah 3:12), and his prediction was fulfilled within forty years. But he claims more than a prophet could. He warns that many will come in his name saying ‘I am he’ (verse 6), which assumes that he alone has the right to that claim. He identifies himself with the Son of Man of Daniel 7:13, the figure who comes with the clouds of heaven and receives an everlasting kingdom from the Ancient of Days. And he gives that figure the roles of Israel's God. In Deuteronomy 30:4 and Zechariah 2:6 it is the LORD who gathers his scattered people from the ends of heaven and the four winds; here the Son of Man sends out the angels, who are his, to gather the elect, who are his (verse 27). Verse 31 makes the claim plain: heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not, which Isaiah 40:8 says of the word of God.

In the same breath he says that the Son does not know the day or the hour (verse 32). The church has read this as part of the full reality of his humanity: the Son who shares the Father's being also shared, in his earthly life, the limits of human knowledge, as Luke 2:52 says he grew in wisdom. The title ‘the Son’, used absolutely beside ‘the Father’, sets him above the angels even in the sentence that states the limit.

The temple whose stones he predicts will fall is being replaced by himself. At his trial false witnesses will claim that he said he would destroy the temple made with hands and build another not made with hands (14:58), and at his death the temple curtain will be torn from top to bottom (15:38). John's Gospel says the temple he spoke of was his body (John 2:21), and Paul calls the church God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16). Finally, the discourse is a map of his own passion. He will be handed over, stand before a council and a governor, be beaten and mocked as a prophet, and be deserted by those closest to him, and the sun will be darkened at noon as he dies. The Son of Man who comes in power is the one who first goes to the cross, and the disciples who are told to endure are following one who endured first.
interpretation:
The church read this chapter from the start as both history and hope. Irenaeus of Lyon (Against Heresies 5.25, around 180) took the abomination standing in the holy place as the Antichrist who will sit in God's temple, joining the saying to Daniel 7 and 2 Thessalonians 2, and so began the futurist reading. Eusebius of Caesarea, in the early fourth century, set Josephus's account of the siege beside Jesus' words to show that they had been fulfilled in AD 70 (Ecclesiastical History 3.5-8), and John Chrysostom, preaching at Antioch around 390, read the shortened days of the Matthean parallel as God's mercy in cutting short the Roman war (Homilies on Matthew 76). In the next homily (77) Chrysostom took ‘this generation’ to mean the generation of believers, not the people then alive. Augustine, answering Bishop Hesychius of Salona in a long letter he later called On the End of the World (Letter 199, around 419), argued that Luke's version showed the abomination fulfilled when Jerusalem was taken, that some of its sayings may describe Christ coming in his church between the first coming and the last, and that no one could calculate the end; he refers back to the letter in City of God 20.5. That threefold reading, the fall of Jerusalem, the coming of Christ in his church, and the final coming, passed into medieval exegesis, and Thomas Aquinas gathered the patristic comments in his Catena Aurea. Calvin's Harmony of the Gospels (1555) held that Christ joined the destruction of Jerusalem and the last judgment in one discourse so that his disciples would live watchfully through both.

Jewish memory of the same events runs through the rabbinic literature. The Mishnah fixes the ninth of Av as the day both temples fell (m. Taanit 4:6), and the fast of Tisha B'Av, with the reading of Lamentations, still keeps it. The Babylonian Talmud tells stories of the war, the feud of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza that led to the revolt, and Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's escape from the besieged city in a coffin to ask Vespasian for Yavneh and its sages (b. Gittin 55b-56b), which became the origin story of rabbinic Judaism after the temple. Another passage says the second temple fell because of baseless hatred among Jews (b. Yoma 9b). These are not comments on Mark, but they show that the catastrophe Jesus predicted was, for his own people, a grief that reshaped their faith.

Modern criticism made the chapter a battleground. Timothée Colani (Jésus-Christ et les croyances messianiques de son temps, 1864) argued that verses 5 to 31 were a Jewish-Christian ‘little apocalypse’ inserted into Jesus' words, a theory that dominated the next century. Albert Schweitzer's Quest of the Historical Jesus (1906) instead made Jesus' expectation of an imminent end the key to his whole ministry. James Stuart Russell (The Parousia, 1878) argued that the coming of Christ in the chapter took place in AD 70, the ancestor of modern preterism. George Beasley-Murray traced the debate in Jesus and the Future (1954) and Jesus and the Last Days (1993), defending the discourse as rooted in Jesus' teaching; Lars Hartman (Prophecy Interpreted, 1966) showed how closely it follows Daniel. R. T. France (2002) and N. T. Wright (Jesus and the Victory of God, 1996) read verses 24 to 27 as the Son of Man's vindication in the judgment on the temple, while most evangelical and Catholic commentators keep a reference to the final return. Popular prophecy took another road: the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) read ‘generation’ as the Jewish race, and Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970) suggested that the generation which saw Israel reborn in 1948 would see the end within about forty years. The long line of failed date-setters, from William Miller's followers in 1844 to Harold Camping in 2011, has been, in effect, a commentary on verse 32.

In worship the chapter belongs to the end and the beginning of the church year. In the Revised Common Lectionary, Year B, verses 1 to 8 are read in November near the year's end and verses 24 to 37 on the First Sunday of Advent; the Roman lectionary reads verses 24 to 32 on the Thirty-third Sunday in Ordinary Time and verses 33 to 37 on the First Sunday of Advent. The temple's fall has been painted from Josephus rather than Mark: Francesco Hayez's Destruction of the Temple of Jerusalem (1867) hangs in the Gallerie dell'Accademia in Venice, and David Roberts's vast Siege and Destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans (1850), now lost, survives in Louis Haghe's lithograph. The Arch of Titus in Rome remains the most sobering illustration of verse 2.
text:
English Bibles differ in a handful of places in this chapter, mostly where the King James Version follows later manuscripts.

In verse 2 Codex Bezae (D), Codex Washingtonianus (W), and several Old Latin manuscripts add ‘and after three days another will rise without hands’, drawn from the saying reported at the trial (14:58) and in John 2:19; no modern version adopts it. In verse 8 the King James Version's ‘famines and troubles’ reflects a word added in later manuscripts; the earliest have only famines. In verse 11 the King James Version adds ‘neither do ye premeditate’, a phrase found in the Textus Receptus and omitted by modern critical editions. In verse 14 the Byzantine manuscripts add ‘spoken of by Daniel the prophet’, taken from Matthew 24:15, and change the masculine participle ‘standing’ to a neuter that agrees with ‘abomination’; the earlier text keeps Mark's deliberate mismatch, which hints that the abomination is a person. In verse 33 many later manuscripts, and the King James Version, read ‘watch and pray’; Codex Vaticanus and Codex Bezae lack ‘and pray’, which was probably borrowed from 14:38. In verse 32 the words ‘nor the Son’ are firm in every early witness to Mark, while in the parallel at Matthew 24:36 many later manuscripts omit them, probably because scribes found them troubling.

Old Testament numbering also differs. The passages from Joel that stand behind verses 24 and 25 are Joel 2:31 and 3:15 in English Bibles, but Joel 3:4 and 4:15 in the Hebrew Bible, which divides that book into four chapters. Readers comparing a Jewish translation with an English Christian Bible will find the same words under different numbers.

teach.big: Jesus prepares his followers for a world of upheaval and persecution not by giving them a timetable but by giving them his word, his Spirit, and his promise to come, so that they refuse deception, endure to the end, and keep watch.

outline.t: What looks permanent is not: the most magnificent religious building of its age would fall, and the disciples' first question is the wrong one, when rather than how to live.
The first danger is not war but deception; disasters are real, but they are birth pains, not proof that God has lost control or that the end has come.
Disciples will be handed over as Jesus was, yet persecution becomes witness, the gospel goes to all nations, the Spirit gives words, and endurance is the mark of the saved.

When the crisis comes, faith flees rather than clings: Jesus grieves for the vulnerable, tells his people to pray about their suffering, and promises that God limits the days for the sake of his chosen.
Signs and wonders do not validate a messiah; Jesus has told us beforehand, and his word is the test.
History does not end in chaos but in the Son of Man, who comes with power and glory and gathers his people from every corner of the earth.
The signs are real and the words are sure; Jesus' promises outlast the universe, and the temple's fall within a generation shows that he keeps his word.
No one knows the day, not even the Son, so every servant does his assigned work and keeps awake; what Jesus says to four, he says to all.

teach.pitfalls:
The commonest misuse of this chapter is to treat it as a code for dating the end, fitting each war, earthquake, or political event to a verse. Jesus says the opposite: wars and earthquakes are ‘not yet the end’ (verse 7), and ‘no one knows about that day or hour’ (verse 32). Preachers who have set dates have always been wrong, and they have damaged the credibility of the gospel and the faith of those who trusted them. A second error runs the other way: explaining away the second coming because some of the chapter refers to AD 70. Even interpreters who read verses 24 to 27 of the temple's fall keep the personal return of Christ, which the creeds confess, and verse 32 at least points to it.

A third pitfall is to present one reading of verses 24 to 30 as the only faithful one. Preterist, futurist, and mixed readings are held by careful interpreters who share the church's confession, and a teacher should say so. A fourth is to read the chapter as if it were about someone else's future. Its warnings about deception, family division, persecution, and sleep were meant for its first hearers and for every generation since, and it ends by saying so (verse 37). Finally, avoid reading the temple's destruction as a verdict against the Jewish people. Jesus speaks as Jeremiah did, from inside Israel, with grief (compare Luke 19:41-44), and the same chapter warns his own followers that they will fall away without watchfulness.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on two kinds of fear. Some listeners have been frightened by end-times preaching, sometimes as children, and carry anxiety about being left behind or missing the signs; they need to hear that Jesus' repeated command is ‘do not be alarmed’ (verse 7) and that his purpose in telling them beforehand was to steady them, not to terrify them. Others know the persecution and family division of verses 9 to 13 from experience: converts rejected by their families, believers who have lost work or safety for their faith, Christians from places where the church suffers. For them the promises of the Spirit's help (verse 11) and God's limit on suffering (verse 20) are not abstractions. Be careful with verse 12 in a room where some have been betrayed by family for other reasons; the verse names the pain honestly without making it a virtue. And for the scrupulous, who fear they are not watching well enough, the parable's picture of watching is simply doing the task each servant has been given.

hard.q: Jesus said this generation would not pass away until all these things happened. Was he mistaken about the time of his return?
hard.a:
The objection is old and serious. Verse 30 sets a time limit in the most solemn form Jesus uses, ‘Truly I tell you’, and every other time Mark uses the word generation he means Jesus' contemporaries. If ‘all these things’ includes the coming of the Son of Man in verse 26, then Jesus predicted that the end would come within his hearers' lifetimes, and it did not. Albert Schweitzer (The Quest of the Historical Jesus, 1906) built his portrait of Jesus as a prophet of the imminent end on sayings like this one and concluded that history had proved him wrong. Bertrand Russell (Why I Am Not a Christian, 1927) cited the expectation as a reason to doubt Jesus' wisdom, and C. S. Lewis, a believer, called verse 30 the most embarrassing verse in the Bible in his essay ‘The World's Last Night’. Jewish readers have long added a related objection: the Messiah was to bring the age of peace the prophets foretold, and the world after Jesus did not see it.

Christian interpreters answer in three main ways, each with able defenders. The preterist reading, argued by J. Stuart Russell (The Parousia, 1878) and in a moderate form by R. T. France and N. T. Wright, holds that verses 5 to 27 describe the events leading to AD 70, that the coming of the Son of Man in verse 26 uses Daniel 7's picture of the Son of Man coming to God to receive a kingdom, and that it was fulfilled in his vindication and the judgment on the temple, all within a generation; the final return is the subject of verses 32 to 37. The futurist reading, common in dispensational teaching and represented by the Scofield Reference Bible (1909), places much of the chapter still ahead and reads genea as the Jewish people or as the generation that sees the signs. The mixed reading, defended by Robert H. Stein (Jesus, the Temple and the Coming Son of Man, 2014) and many commentators, notes that ‘these things’ in verse 29 are signs seen before the end and cannot include the coming itself, so ‘all these things’ in verse 30 means the signs and the temple's fall, which did happen within forty years, while ‘that day’ in verse 32 is the undated final coming. Each view carries a burden: the critical view must explain why Mark preserved a saying he knew had failed, the futurist must answer Mark's own use of genea, and the preterist and mixed views must explain how closely verse 30 follows verses 24 to 27. The timing of Christ's return is a second-order question on which faithful Christians differ; that he will come is confessed by all.

hard.q: How can the Son not know the day or hour, if he is God?
hard.a:
The strongest form of the objection was pressed in the fourth century. If the Son does not know what the Father knows, he cannot share the Father's being, and so he must be a lesser, created being. The followers of Arius used verse 32 in exactly this way, as Athanasius reports in his third Oration against the Arians, and the verse has remained a standard proof text for groups that deny the full deity of Christ, including Jehovah's Witnesses. A Jewish or skeptical reader can press the point from the other side: a God who does not know something is not God, so a Jesus who confesses ignorance has disproved the church's claim for him.

The church's classical answer, given by Athanasius and by Gregory of Nazianzus (Oration 30.15, the Fourth Theological Oration, around 380), is that the Son spoke of ignorance according to the human nature he truly took on, not according to his divine nature, and that the Gospels' willingness to record such a limit is evidence for the reality of his humanity (compare Luke 2:52, where he grows in wisdom). The Council of Chalcedon (451) confessed two natures, divine and human, in one person without confusion or division, and later theologians such as Thomas Aquinas explained verse 32 within that framework. In the nineteenth century kenotic theologians, among them the German Lutheran Gottfried Thomasius and the Anglican Charles Gore (The Incarnation of the Son of God, Bampton Lectures, 1891), drew on Philippians 2:7 to argue that the Son voluntarily limited the use of his divine knowledge in becoming man; many Reformed and Catholic theologians have judged that theory to go too far, and it remains contested. Others note that Jesus' saying still places the Son above the angels and alone beside the Father. The creeds confess that he is truly God and truly man; how best to describe the knowledge of the incarnate Son is a question Christians who share that confession still discuss.

observe: List every command Jesus gives in this chapter (see to it, do not be alarmed, flee, pray, be on your guard, keep watch). What do they have in common?
What two questions do the disciples ask in verse 4, and which parts of Jesus' answer seem to address each?
Trace the words handed over, hour, sleeping, and watch from this chapter into chapter 14. Where do they reappear?
interpret: Why does Jesus begin his answer about the end with a warning against deception rather than with a sign?
How do verses 30 and 32 fit together? What difference does the shift from ‘those days’ to ‘that day’ make?
Why might Mark place this discourse immediately before the passion narrative?
apply: What impressive things in your life or culture feel permanent but are not, and how would Jesus' words in verse 2 change the way you hold them?
How can you tell the difference between faithful watchfulness and anxious speculation about the end, and which one shapes your reading of the news?
Each servant in the parable has an assigned task while the master is away. What is the task you have been given, and what would it mean to be found awake in it?
